title: Trump Plaza Casino Opens Amid Labor Violations
description_short: Trump Plaza Casino Opens Amid Labor Violations
description_medium: Trump Plaza Hotel and Casino opened in Atlantic City in May 1984. Its title associates the opening with labor violations, but the linked UPI report concerns Trump Castle and Plaza Chapter 11 filings in 1992, eight years later. That article does not substantiate the construction, contractor-lien or minority-hiring claims in the populated summary.
subcategory: Trump Plaza opening and construction labor

preserved_fields.title: Trump Plaza Casino Opens Amid Labor Violations
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Plaza Casino Opens Amid Labor Violations
preserved_fields.description_medium: Trump Plaza Hotel and Casino opened in Atlantic City in May 1984, but the construction and opening were marred by disputes with contractors and documented labor violations. Multiple contractors filed liens against Trump for unpaid work, a pattern that would repeat across Trump's real estate portfolio throughout the 1980s. The casino was also cited for failing to meet minority hiring commitments. The New Jersey Casino Control Commission repeatedly investigated Trump's properties for labor and regulatory violations during this period.

notes: I read the linked UPI article. It reports 1992 bankruptcies for Trump Castle and Trump Plaza, not the 1984 opening or the labor and minority-hiring claims in the populated medium. Proposed correction: source the 1984 opening and each labor allegation separately; otherwise retitle to the 1992 bankruptcy story.
proposed_correction: Trump Plaza’s 1984 Opening; Labor Allegations Need a Relevant Source

title: Gaetz Withdraws, Pam Bondi Nominated
description_medium: On November 21, 2024, President-elect Donald Trump named former Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi as his new choice to lead the Justice Department, hours after Matt Gaetz withdrew from consideration. NBC News reported that Gaetz’s withdrawal followed intensified scrutiny over sexual-misconduct allegations. Bondi’s nomination was a separate appointment decision; the linked article does not establish claims about her earlier investigation of Trump University.
description_long: On November 21, 2024, President-elect Donald Trump selected former Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi as his nominee for U.S. attorney general, hours after Matt Gaetz withdrew his name from consideration. NBC News reported that Gaetz’s withdrawal followed increased scrutiny over allegations of sexual misconduct. Bondi had served as Florida’s attorney general from 2011 to 2019 and was a longtime Trump ally. Trump said he wanted her to refocus the Justice Department, which he had accused of being weaponized against him. The article noted that, if confirmed by the Senate, Bondi would lead federal investigations and prosecutions; at the time of the announcement, she was a nominee rather than the confirmed attorney general. This entry concerns the change in Trump’s choice after Gaetz withdrew. The linked report does not cover Bondi’s earlier role in a Trump University investigation or establish that a campaign contribution caused any prosecutorial decision, so those claims in the populated medium are omitted from this account.
subcategory: Attorney general nomination after Gaetz withdrawal

preserved_fields.title: Gaetz Withdraws, Pam Bondi Nominated
preserved_fields.description_medium: Facing intense opposition even from within the GOP over his sex trafficking allegations, Matt Gaetz withdrew his nomination for Attorney General in November 2024. Trump quickly replaced him with Pam Bondi, the former Florida Attorney General. Bondi had previously dropped an investigation into Trump University after receiving a $25,000 campaign contribution from Trump's foundation, highlighting a history of transactional loyalty.

notes: I read the linked NBC News report. It supports Gaetz’s withdrawal and Trump’s same-day selection of Bondi, and attributes the scrutiny to allegations. It does not support the populated medium’s claim that a donation caused Bondi to end an investigation of Trump University; that unrelated allegation is not repeated.

title: Transition Team Fires Federal Workers
description_medium: The Guardian reported in February 2025 that the Trump administration had sent termination notices to probationary federal employees after Trump took office. Some workers said letters cited poor performance despite positive reviews, while the White House said it was removing noncritical staff. The linked report does not support the title’s claim that Trump’s transition team fired workers before inauguration.
description_long: A Guardian report published on February 21, 2025, described the Trump administration’s dismissal of thousands of probationary federal employees after the president took office. It reported cases at the Interior Department and other agencies, where workers said termination notices cited poor performance despite positive reviews. The White House defended the reductions as removals of employees it considered noncritical. The story also described confusion as officials tried to reverse some terminations and quoted a labor lawyer who warned that the dismissals could expose the government to significant legal costs. These events concern personnel actions by the administration after inauguration. They do not establish that Trump’s transition team sent notices before he took office or that the actions implemented Schedule F early, as the populated title and medium claim. The entry needs to distinguish the source-supported February terminations from any separate pre-inauguration notices. A corrected title should identify the post-inauguration probationary-worker firings unless another source documents transition-team notices and their legal basis.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

preserved_fields.title: Transition Team Fires Federal Workers
preserved_fields.description_medium: Before Trump even officially took office, his transition team sent out notices terminating thousands of federal workers, attempting to enforce the 'Schedule F' classification early. The unprecedented and legally dubious move bypassed standard civil service protections and created chaos across federal agencies, jumpstarting his campaign to gut the 'deep state.'

notes: I read the linked Guardian report. It concerns probationary-employee firings after Trump took office, including notices citing poor performance and confusion over attempted reversals. It does not support a transition-team action before inauguration or an early Schedule F implementation. Proposed correction: retitle around the post-inauguration firings or provide a source for the pre-inauguration notices.
proposed_correction: Trump Administration Fires Probationary Federal Employees After Inauguration

description_short: Budget Proposes Medicaid Cuts: 13 Million to Lose Coverage

The supplied notes say it does not support attributing a 13-million coverage loss to the March proposal. The linked page returned HTTP 403, and the proposal, estimate and hospital-impact claims need matching sources.

preserved_fields.title: Budget Proposes Medicaid Cuts: 13 Million to Lose Coverage
preserved_fields.description_short: Budget Proposes Medicaid Cuts: 13 Million to Lose Coverage
preserved_fields.description_medium: In March 2025, the Trump administration's budget proposal included provisions that independent analyses projected would result in 13 million Americans losing Medicaid coverage. The cuts were achieved through work requirements, per capita caps on federal Medicaid spending, and elimination of certain expansion populations. Hospitals in rural areas warned the cuts would force closures. Medical associations, patient advocacy groups, and even some Republican senators in Medicaid-heavy states expressed opposition. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the proposals would reduce federal Medicaid spending by over $800 billion over a decade.

notes: The linked CBO report is an estimate for H.R. 1, not a March 2025 budget proposal, and returned HTTP 403. The supplied notes say the available estimates differ by bill version and date and do not substantiate this synopsis’s 13-million figure or combined work-requirement, per-capita-cap and hospital-closure claims. Proposed correction: identify the exact proposal and date, then cite its corresponding CBO estimate; do not combine separate bill versions or enrollment projections.
proposed_correction: Medicaid Coverage-Loss Projection Needs a Bill-Specific CBO Source
